paragraphs.text:
OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, ARCHBISHOP OF ANTIOCH AND MARTYR: ON THE HEXAEMERON

Clement, then, and Africanus, and besides them Tatian, and of those of the circumcision Josephus and Justus, have recorded that the divine Moses flourished in the time of Inachus, each of them offering his own proof from ancient history. Inachus precedes the Trojan War by seven hundred years. But one of the saints, who made a most exact [reckoning] of the times, found that it was the most holy Jacob who flourished together with the times of Inachus, whereas Josephus [dated] Moses [there] [?]. For he devised the composition of a chronological table in parallel columns and set side by side the rulers of each nation. He collected the dates of the kingdoms of the Chaldeans, Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Lydians, Hebrews, Egyptians, Athenians, Argives, Sicyonians, Lacedaemonians, Corinthians, Thessalians, Macedonians, and Latins, who were later called Romans. And [bringing] their dates to the same [?] … the dates of the kings of each nation, he set the years of the kingdom of the Assyrian queen, that is, of Semiramis, against the years of Abraham. For blessed Abraham was known in the time of Semiramis; Joseph [?] in the time of Inachus; and Moses in the time of Cecrops, whom … three hundred years before the Trojan events … the children of the Greeks [call] the first [king] of Attica. Thus Moses is the oldest of the ancient sages known to the Greeks, older, he says, than Homer and Hesiod and the Trojan War, than Heracles, Musaeus and Linus, and also Chiron, Orpheus, the Dioscuri, Asclepius, Dionysus, Hermes and Apollo, than the Greek mysteries and rites, and the very deeds of Zeus; older too than the flood in the time of Deucalion, the conflagration in the time of Phaethon, the birth of Erichthonius from Hephaestus and Earth, and the rape of Kore. For all these

came after Cecrops. Homer and Hesiod fall many [years] below him in time, and those who are later than these are surely much later still than the age of Moses. This man, then, was shown to be the most divine teacher of truth to all the wise. For, spurning the so-called wisdom of the Egyptians, he set forth excellently how this world was constituted, being inspired with the truth, plainly, by the very God who is over all and Creator of the universe. For he says: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." And many among the Greeks who dared to set forth the contrary were hurled into an abyss of ignorance. For doctrines put forward from human thinking are … [?] and without ballast. Among them no argument has stood unshaken, since each successor always overthrows the one before him; so that the faithful have no work in refuting their views, since they are quite enough to overturn one another. What the heaven is like in shape and substance Isaiah teaches us, saying: "He who set up the heaven like a vault," hinting that it is fine, not solid or thick, as he also says elsewhere: "He who established the heaven like smoke." And the psalm says that the earth is set upon the waters: "He himself founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers." How this is so we must not curiously inquire, but believe. For the simplicity of faith is stronger than logical demonstrations, since God's judgments are beyond reach and beyond comprehension. On the first day, then, God made the heaven and the earth and the light, and lit up all things in a swift instant; and this is the perishable light. For before this, darkness enclosed everything like a shadow, since the heaven had been stretched around it and had made all that it contained, and the space left within, lightless. Outside the heaven, however, there is light without shadow, incorruptible and eternal, in which the angels dwell; of it Solomon says, "Light for the righteous always," and in it those who have lived well also take their rest. You will understand how this is arranged from a clear example: inextinguishable light shines over the space outside the heaven, while gloom enclosed the space within before the light came into being. For just as when someone at steady noon pitches a tent of dense material, he creates an improvised darkness, and the space enclosed can in no way be lit unless a gleam of light shines into it; so such an insubstantial darkness enclosed the world covered by the heaven, and God dispersed it by creating the light, naming it day and the darkness night. For when light is poured out, day comes; when it is drawn in, night succeeds it. Hence in reckoning time, too, we count days and not nights.

On the second day God made the firmament. This is something other than the heaven made in the beginning. Some have said that it is the same: the second, they say, is an elaboration, because there the making of earth and heaven is related as in summary, while here Scripture relates in more detail how it came about. But we say they are two different things, since a different name and a particular function are given for the second heaven. This one, then, is different from the one made in the beginning, being of a more solid nature. "And God divided between the water which was under the firmament" [and the water above it]. For he divided the nature of the waters, which was boundless, so that it is both above the firmament and below. The aether is fiery and scorching, and would consume the whole of the dry land were it not held back by the boundary set by its Maker. It is for this reason, too, that there is water in the air, carried by the clouds from the vapors that rise up, vapors which the rivers, springs, lakes and all the seas send up, so that the aether may not make everything red-hot and consume it. Rain comes about in this way: the exhalations gather on high, the air is condensed by the pressure of the winds, and the moisture scattered through the cloud draws together and becomes drops, and by the weight of what has been compacted they are carried downward. Snow forms from the waters in this way: the moisture, beaten back by the force of the winds, froths up; and being beaten through and through, it is chilled and freezes; and when the cloud breaks, the snow falls. Thunder [arises] on the same principle: … a collision occurs, and this, driven about in the hollows of the clouds and bursting out violently, produces the sound of thunder. On the third day, at God's command, the water was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared. "And he called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called seas." It was gathered into one gathering for this reason: so that … from the places where it is … and overflowing it might not cover the land. This is why the sea, often raging under the winds and rising to the greatest height in its waves, no sooner touches the shores than it dissolves its onrush into foam and turns back, bridled by sand, the weakest of all things. Otherwise, what prevented the Red Sea from flooding all of Egypt, which lies lower than it, and joining the neighboring sea, if it had not been fettered by the command of the Creator? That this is true Sesostris the Egyptian and Darius the Mede have proved to us by experience. For they attempted to join the Egyptian and the Indian seas and could not, so much lower than the Red Sea does Egypt lie. He commanded, then, that it be gathered into one gathering, and that no other sea should arise from it, but that it should remain in the first collection. For many were …

[?] and the ravines. The words "and the gatherings of the waters he called seas" refer to the gulfs left by the surrounding land, each according to its own shape: such as the northern sea, the southern sea, the eastern and western seas, and their particular names: the Pontus, the Aegean, the Ionian, the Sardinian, the Sicilian, the Tyrrhenian. It was not any chance collection of waters that came together into one sea, or system, but the greatest and most prominent ones; for we must not understand marshes and lakes to be included. For just as fire is both broken up into small portions and also poured out in a mass beneath the air, so it is with water: even if there are some small, separate collections, yet there is one gathering, which sets the whole element apart from the others. For the water of the sea is the source of all the moisture throughout the earth. The whole earth is channelled beneath, and the water is distributed through hidden passages, as certain cavernous places on land show. For the flowing sea, running through narrow places, when it is caught in crooked and steep outlets and pushed by the force of the wind, breaks through the surface of the earth, and coming out becomes drinkable, changed into sweetness by being filtered. Again, when it is caught on its way out in hot places, drawn up by the wind for the same reason, it comes out boiling. The sea is also the source of the waters in the air: for its waters, drawn up through the clouds, warmed by the sun's ray, chilled by the shade of the cloud, and cleared by the very height, become sweet and sprinkle the land. On the same day God also commanded the earth to sprout the herb of grass, "sowing seed according to its kind, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit, whose seed is in it." And even now the order in which plants grow bears witness to that first arrangement. For sprouting comes before every herb and every grass: when the earth has moisture and warmth in due measure, the seed is cast into it and becomes loose and fertile; and beginning from the earth around it, it draws to itself what is proper and akin to it, and being fattened, it spreads further, so that it roots downward and peeps up upward, putting forth as many stalks as it has roots. As the shoot is continually warmed, the moisture drawn up through the roots by the heat brings with it the nourishment of the earth; and this is distributed into the stalk and the husk, into the sheaths of the grain, into the grain itself and the awns. The stalk of wheat is girded with knots, so that like ligaments they may bear the weight of the ears. The stalk is also hollow, so that it may serve as a sheath for the grain, and so that the grain may not be easily plundered by birds that pick up seeds. And it has put forth the awns in place of darts, to ward off harm from small creatures. Oats are hollow throughout, since their head is not heavy. And if

poisonous plants sprang up together with the food plants, such as hellebore, aconite, mandrake and the juice of the poppy, none of these has been left useless. Starlings feed on hemlock because of the make of their bodies: since the passages to their heart are narrow, they get rid of what they have swallowed in time. Quails eat hellebore and suffer no harm, having a peculiar constitution. With mandrake physicians induce sleep, and with opium they lull violent pains to rest. With hemlock they wither frenzied appetites, and with hellebore they soothe chronic ailments. "And the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit." All things sprang up from the earth in a single instant, though they had not existed before, each with its own property and each recognizable by its own character. The olive, the palm and the cypress grow to a great height. Some of these do not have many knots or many branches, like the fir and the cypress, and sometimes the palm too. Evergreen are the olive, the palm, the laurel, the myrtle, the pine, the cypress, the fir, the juniper, the thuja, and the one the Arcadians call philodrys; also the phyleos [?], the cedar, the stone pine, the box, the holm oak, the vetch and the chickling. The rose then sprouted without the thorn; afterwards the thorn was joined to the beauty of the flower, so that, having pain set beside delight, we might remember the sin through which the earth was condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles for us. The almond is the first to blossom but the last to bear its fruit. If the bitter almond has its trunk bored through near the root and receives a resinous wedge of pine driven into the middle of the pith, it changes its unpleasant juices into an edible sweetness. The sour pomegranate, too, given the same treatment, turns sweet. The female palm lets her branches droop, as though longing for union with the male; and the farmers, placing the male's blossom-clusters on her branches, restore her to her proper upright shape. The [?] sprouts late, but does not lag behind the others in bearing fruit. The olive, the linden, the white poplar and the elms turn their leaves upside down after the summer solstice, and by this everyone knows that the summer solstice has come. The farmers keep the fruit of the cultivated fig from dropping in this way: they tie [?] on it the unripe fruit of the wild fig, and so make it stay on without falling. For the tiny creature inside the unripe fig settles on the base of the fig and keeps off the outer breeze blowing round it, so that the fig does not spoil and fall. Since the fruit of the fig is tender, it is covered with thick leaves; but the walnut's, being hard, is sheltered by a light covering of leaves. For this reason, too, the vine leaf is split, so that the cluster may both escape harm from the air and admit the sun's ray through its openings. Thus nothing is idle; God has ordered all things with ineffable

wisdom. For a single water, carried or drawn up through the root, nourishes the trunk in one way, the pith in another, the bark in another, the wood in another, and the root itself in another; and from the same moisture wine is formed in the vine, oil in the olive, and something else in another plant. And among the sweet fruits themselves the variety of richness is beyond telling: the sweetness of the vine is one thing, that of the apple another, and that of the fig and the palm something else again. The tears of trees, too, differ from one another: the tear of the mastic is one thing, and the juice of the balsam another, which is the finest of all perfumes and grows in abundance around Jericho. When the local people cut it from the bushes with a sharp stone, the juice yields [?]. Some also report that amber is the juice of plants, hardened into the nature of stone. On the fourth day God created the two great lights, the sun and the moon, in the firmament of heaven, to give light upon the earth, to divide between the day and the night. This light of the sun was prepared as a vehicle for that firstborn light. For as fire is one thing and the lamp another, the one having the power to give light, the other that of displaying it to those who need it; and as whiteness is one thing and the whitened body another, so these, though different in nature, are united by the power of the Creator. And let no one think that day and the sun are the same. For first the Creator made simple light, which he also called day, and then the sun, composed of fire and light. For just as we see that the earth has fire created in its very bosom, so the sun has light; for light combined with fire made the sun most brilliant. But perhaps someone will object: "How is this evident, when the division is not seen? For light is not seen on its own, nor fire on its own." Let such a person learn how many things fire puts forth within itself: brightness, heat, yellowness. By separating these the all-wise Craftsman reveals that they are compounded. For when he wishes to warm a living creature, he takes the heat of fire, and the creature has its heat but not its light. But when heat has been separated from brightness in the creature, he takes, in turn, the yellowness; and we see the yellowness, but no longer the heat and the shining. And again he separates off the heat and gives the brightness alone, as one can see in lightning, which in flashing only gives light and does not also warm. The same example holds for the moon too. For it also becomes more visible when lit by the sun, just as the sun does by the day. For the appearance of the moon is like a coal, as one can see at an eclipse: when the sun withdraws its own light from it, it renders it dim; but when it lights it up, it makes it full. For the moon, as it were, puts on the light of the sun and becomes brighter; and in the same way the sun, putting on the light of the day, becomes more brilliant, though that day neither

burns nor warms, but only gives light. That the sun consists of fire is clear from its burning and scorching. "To divide between the day and the night": that is, he assigned the sun to the measures of the day and the moon to those of the night. Night is the shadow of the earth when the sun is hidden. For just as in the daytime, when something blocks the light, a shadow arises and the light [?] beneath it, so night arises when the air around the earth is shaded. And the sun keeps hidden within itself forever the light it received from its Maker in the beginning; but not so the moon, which continually puts it off, waxing and waning. "And let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years." The sun and moon generate this time. For their courses, drawn along in due measure, produce the ordered progressions of the seasons. It is called time because it rolls round as on a circle in orderly successions one after another, the first to the second, and the third to the next. "Let them be for signs," because they always foretell the coming of a storm: for when a haze forms in the air, it dims the rays of the sun, and the sun looks like a coal and blood-red, unable to disperse the air thickened by the vapors of the earth; and from this a sign of storm is given. When the so-called haloes (these are certain round outlines like a threshing floor, from which they take their name) surround the sun, violent winds are signaled; and when the so-called parhelia accompany the sun's course, it is a sign of disturbances in the air; and again, when streaks like rods, of the color of the rainbow, appear stretched [?] across the clouds, rains or storms or a more lasting change in the weather are signaled. As for the moon, when on the third day it shows itself thin and clear in its horns, it promises settled fair weather; but when it appears thick in its horns and reddish, it announces heavy rain or a violent south wind. The sun and moon, then, are instruments of time: of days, months and years; and the stars [are signs] of months, of sowing and of harvest

The Pleiades, when they rise, show the season of harvest, and when they set, that of sowing. And together with the Wagon they serve as a sign to sailors; for the stars serve as signs and pointers of places. The Bear shows the north; one who looks toward the rising of the Pleiades [?] finds that their point shows the north; when the Bear itself turns, its horn shows the east; and the bright part of the moon indicates the east. Before these there was no time, but an interval, a long and timeless age. So much, then, has been said about signs. By seasons we take it to mean the alternations of the

…seasons: winter, spring, summer and autumn. Winter comes when the sun lingers in the southern regions and casts a long night-shadow over our part of the world, so that the air around the earth is chilled, and the moist vapours condense and become the causes of rain, frost and snow. But when the sun returns from the southern regions and reaches the middle, there is an equinox; and the longer it lingers over our regions, the more it gradually restores a mild climate, and spring comes, bringing sprouting to plants and new life to trees. From there the sun runs on toward the summer solstice, up to the Bear itself, and brings us the long days. Because it is in closer contact with the air, it [?] the air, dries out the whole earth and ripens every fruit, being at its most fiery, and it makes the shadows short, since it shines down from on high. For on the shortest days the shadows are longest. And when it passes back again from the northern regions to the southern, autumn comes, as the great heat gradually fades and winter approaches without doing harm. But the sun does not make the day—let no one suppose that, for day and night are older than the sun. It only rules over the day, as the psalmist declares to us: "He made," he says, "the sun to rule the day, the moon and the stars to rule the night." The sun has this rule because it carries the light around within itself: whenever it rises above our horizon, it scatters the darkness and brings the day. The moon, when it has completed its course twelve times, makes a year, except that it needs an intercalary month to keep exact pace with the seasons. For the solar year is the sun's return, by its own motion, from a given point back to the same point. When the moon wanes, the bodies of living creatures grow thin and become somewhat hollow; when it waxes, they fill out again. This is because the moon secretly instils moisture mixed with warmth: people who sleep under the moon have their heads filled with excess moisture, and freshly slaughtered meat and anything of that kind quickly spoils when the moonlight falls on it. Disturbances in the air also arise from this kind of cause. For at the new moon, even when there is a settled calm, sudden storms of wind arise, as the clouds are shaken and collide with one another; the currents in the straits ebb and flow, and around the ocean the sea surges back. And if an eclipse of the sun happens at the new moon, it is more complete, for the moon passes beneath the sun and blocks its rays. The moon itself is something great. Yet silly tales told by drunken old women have survived everywhere, that by certain sorceries the moon is moved from its proper seat and brought down to earth. And what place could have received it if it had been brought down? Do not

be deceived by its appearance into thinking it is something small. Our sight, becoming small, has made the things we see seem small as well, transferring its own condition to the objects it sees. If someone on a mountain ridge looks at plains with cattle grazing together on them, does he not seem to see something like ants? For sight, spent in the air and fading out, is not enough for an exact perception of what it sees. That the body of the moon is enormous can be learned from the evidence. Cities throughout the inhabited world, very far apart from one another, whose streets face east, all receive the moonlight equally, and people living in the west and in the southern and northern regions see it alike. On the fifth day God commanded the waters to bring forth creeping things with living souls according to their kind, and at once the sea gave birth to every different kind of creature. Of the creatures of the sea, some are amphibious, such as seals, crocodiles and hippopotamuses, and also frogs and crabs, which, however, cannot swim: they are crawlers by nature and are dragged along by the movement of the water. Others bear live young, such as seals, dolphins, electric rays and the like. God merely gave the command, and the sea brought forth the creatures of the open sea and of the shore, of the depths and of the rocks, those that go in shoals and those that live alone, the sea monsters, the huge creatures and the tiniest of fishes, all having a natural kinship with water. For if they are separated from the water even for a little while, they die, having no breath: the opening and closing of their gills, which take in the water and let it pass through, serves them as breath. None of them has teeth on only one side; all are thickly set with sharp teeth, so that their food does not slip away during long chewing. For if they chewed it fine, the water would destroy it. None of them chews the cud except the parrotfish. Their food, too, differs, each having what suits it. Some feed on mud, others on seaweed, others on the plants that grow in the water, and still others eat one another. They also have various peculiar traits. The sawfish has long wings. When it sees a ship sailing before the wind, it too raises its wings, imitates the ship's movements and races the sailors. Then, after covering forty stades and growing tired, it lowers its wings and is carried by the waves to the place

The sea monster is called the aspidochelone by some. It is by nature enormous, so that it often gives sailors the impression of a large island. When it surfaces from the deep, its body looks like rough rocks, and sailors drive stakes into it and moor their boats there. These boats are immediately sunk when the monster, heated through by the [?], [?] into the deep

[?]. By nature it also has a deep voice, and when it is hungry it opens its mouth and gives off a most fragrant smell, so that small fish are drawn in and leap whole into its mouth. Because of its size it lives in the Atlantic seas. The crab finds the flesh of the oyster good to eat. Since it cannot force open the closed shells, it watches for the oyster to open its valves in sheltered places as it basks in the sunlight; then it takes a pebble, slips it in secretly and stops the shell from closing, and so easily [?] it

The sea urchin knows in advance when a storm is coming, and it creeps under a pebble so as not to be tossed about by the force of the waves. The octopus, when it comes near a rock, takes on the same colour as the rock and devours the fish that come close to it. The remora is very small by nature, yet it stops the largest ships even when they are running before a fair wind, so that the ship seems to be fixed fast in the open sea. In the river there is the hydrus, which has the shape of a dog; it is the crocodile's enemy and kills it while it sleeps. The crocodile sleeps with its mouth wide open, and the hydrus rolls itself in mud, [?] into its mouth, and kills it by devouring all its [?]. The crocodile is both a beast and a fish. It is long from head to tail, but its width is not in proportion to its length. Its hide is wrinkled scale; the colour of its back is like black rock, and its belly like white rock. It has four feet, curving gently outward to the side like those of the land tortoise, and a long, thick tail, which is the end of its spine, a single bone. Along the top the tail is cut into spines like the teeth of a saw, and it strikes with it whatever it is fighting. It has a single head joined onto its back and set in one straight line with it. As long as it is not gaping, it is the head of a beast; but when it gapes, it becomes all mouth, the opening reaching to the shoulders

The so-called hippopotamus has the feet and belly of a horse, but a cloven hoof like an ox's, and a thick tail bare of hair, as indeed is its whole body. Its head is round, differing a little from a horse's cheek. It has gaping nostrils that breathe out fiery smoke as from a furnace, and a broad jaw, for it opens its mouth right up to the temples. Inside, its mouth is packed with three rows of teeth, and besides these it has two curved tusks like a boar's. It is extremely greedy, feeding on crops. It is hunted by the following trick. The hunters watch where it goes, dig a pit, roof it over with straw and heap sand on top, and down below they set up a wooden chamber with its doors open toward the top of the pit

[?]. The beast steps on it unsuspecting, falls in, and is carried down and shut inside the chamber, and the hunters lock it in at once. Second [?]… The beast is the size of an ox. Fish have great and intense heat within them; this is why they digest what they eat quickly, the food rotting at once in their stomachs. The sea fox, when it cannot escape capture and has swallowed the hook, leaps out and runs back up the line, bites through it and gets away. The crocodile is a man-eating beast. When it is about to mate, it swims up and turns the female over onto her back on the riverbank, for it alone is made to mate on its back; and after mating it lifts her with its forefeet and turns her back over. But when it suspects that she has been with another male, it pretends to mate with her, turns her over in the same way, and knows by the smell (for it has a very keen sense of smell for this) that she has been defiled by another. Then it tears open her belly with its claws and devours everything inside her. For the animal is soft around the belly, while its back is clothed in dense scales, so that even the sharpest iron brought against it is blunted. "Let the waters bring forth birds with living souls": and all at once the air was filled with birds of every kind. He gave them their origin from the waters, since they have been allotted a certain kinship with fish. For as fish cut through the water with the movement of their fins and swim through it, so birds swim through the air with their wings. Some of them are carnivorous and have a build suited to their way of life: sharp talons, a hooked beak and swift wings, so that they can easily snatch their prey and tear it apart. Others gather seeds, and others feed on anything. The build of each of these kinds differs. Some have no leader and govern themselves; others are ranked under a leader. Some are migratory, and others stay in their own country. The cock is proud, while the hawk is very friendly toward human beings. It is reported that the hawks in Thrace join bird-catchers in the hunt. They make their haunts in very thick woods, where many kinds of birds live, and they team up with the men going out to hunt, in order to receive an equal share of the catch. When the hunters shake the trees, the birds are startled, take fright and fly up, and the hawks, flying over their heads,

strike their heads with their beaks, hurl them to the ground and make the catch easy for the men; and the men gladly give them a share of the catch at once. The pelican loves its young. While it is feeding its chicks, they strike it in the face with their wings, and it pecks at them and kills them. Then, moved with pity, it mourns them for three days. Then the mother comes, stands over them, tears open her side and lets her blood drip onto the chicks, and they are brought back to life. These pelicans eat shellfish in the following way. Since they cannot get at them because the shells are tightly closed, they first swallow them, so that the heat of the throat melts the glue that holds them shut and the loosened shells open. Then they vomit them up and easily eat the edible part. Ringdoves do not brood where they lay their eggs; because there are so many hunters, they move to another place and rear their chicks there. And when they notice that people have come to hunt their chicks, they fly up and draw the hunters' attention onto themselves, giving the chicks a chance to escape; and once the chicks have escaped, they boldly take off together with them and travel through the sky. The peacock, which comes from India, loves beauty. Raising its beauty aloft and putting its feathers on show, it draws the female to mating, displaying this adornment to her like a meadow, for the peacock is almost more flowery than a meadow. Gold is set all over its feathers, and sea-purple runs around the gold in a circle, and beneath the gold lies a circle of equal size, and there is an eye in the feather. The phoenix is the size of a peacock, but it surpasses the peacock in the beauty of its colouring, for its feathers are blended with gold and purple, and its head is naturally adorned with a shapely circle like a crown. The circle is dark blue and like roses. It is beautiful to look at, and, streaming with rays, it stands on high like the sun. Others too have recorded the form of its body, and in their description they put it like this: "Its length is nearly twice an eagle's. Its body is adorned with many-coloured feathers and hues. Its breast appears purple, its legs [?], and at the neck it is decked with saffron [?]. Its head is like [?], and it gazed out with a quince-yellow eye; its pupil [?] appeared like a scarlet berry. It had the most splendid voice of all. It appeared to be the king of all birds, as one could see, for all the winged creatures together rushed after it in a long train behind. Out in front it walked like a proud bull, lifting its feet in a swift stride." They say that this creature is unique, not

kept in existence by succession, but existing entirely alone, and that it lives five hundred years. When it is about to die (for it senses its end beforehand), it picks out some high place facing the sunrise and builds its nest of aromatic twigs. Then it is wholly burned up by the sun's rays and completely reduced to ashes. From the ashes a worm arises, and the worm changes back into the original phoenix. The eagle is most unjust in rearing its young. When it has hatched two, it keeps one as its own, but beats the other with its wings and drives it away, because of the labour of feeding it, as they say. The ossifrage takes in the rejected chick and rears it together with its own young. When the eagle has reared its chick, it flies with it, taking it up into the upper air. If it sees the chick gazing keenly into the brightness of the sun and boldly swimming through the air, it keeps it as its own; but if the chick is too weak for these things, it casts it off as a bastard. They say that when the eagle grows old its eyes grow dim and its wings heavy. It goes to a spring, then flies up into the upper air, where its wings are scorched by the sun and it regains its sight. Then it immediately comes down to the spring, dips itself three times, and is renewed. That, they say, is why the psalm says: "Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's." The vulture conceives by the wind and knows no union with a male, and it lives a hundred years. It lodges in high, lofty places, and no one knows where it makes its home. When it is pregnant, it goes to India and takes the stone called the "easy-birth stone"; when the labour pains seize it, it sits on the stone and gives birth. The stone is round like a nut, and when it is moved it gives out a sound like a bell, because another stone moves inside it. They say that if the vulture is anointed with [?] perfumes it dies. They also say that it does not harm seeds or ravage any living thing, and does not go near a dead bird because of their kinship. And whenever men line up for war, they say, it follows them and does not leave them, since it is a flesh-eater. Storks both arrive at a single signal and

hands over the leadership of the journey. While they sleep, one of them goes around all the others keeping guard. When it has completed a sufficient stretch of its watch, it cries out and turns to sleep, and another in turn takes over this duty. Geese are wakeful by nature and have sharp hearing, quickly sensing the approach of anyone at all, or of anyone with hostile intent. Thus, when enemies had crept in through tunnels and were about to take the great city of Rome, the geese saved it by the natural keenness of their senses, betraying the attackers to the guards by crying out all together. The halcyon is a sea bird, and it nests on the seashore in the middle of winter. While it is brooding, the winds are lulled to sleep and the sea stays perfectly calm for as long as seven days, though before that strong winds were stirring up the sea. And when it has hatched its chicks, God again grants calm weather for another seven days, so that it may rear them. The partridge is crafty, jealous and mischievous, helping hunters to catch their prey. It steals other birds' eggs and hatches them; but when the chicks have grown, each flies off to its own kind, and they leave it alone. The dove is lustful. In India there is a tree called the peridexion, which bears sweet fruit; the doves delight in this tree and make their home in it. The serpent is the dove's enemy, but it is afraid of the tree and does not come near it: to whichever side of the tree the shadow falls, the serpent flees in fear. The doves move to that side, into the shade, for if they leave the shade they are killed by the serpent. The nature of the dove is worth marvelling at. When its neck catches the sun's rays, it shows itself varied with countless shades of colour: crimson, blue, flame-coloured, coal-black, pale yellow and red, and every other kind of colour. The crow loves its young and has only one mate. When it has reared its chicks, it does not stop caring for them and feeding them, and it always flies with them. When building its nest, it carries twigs in its mouth and mud on its wing: it wets the tip of its wing in water and rolls it in fine dust, and in this way contrives a supply of mud. Binding the twigs together little by little with the mud as if with a kind of glue, it builds its nest and rears its chicks. Their feet are broad and webbed, so that they can swim easily in the water, pushing it aside with the webs of their feet as if with oars. The swan has a neck longer than its feet, so that it can draw fish up from the depths. Many birds change their voice and their colour each year. The blackbird turns from black to tawny, and from a songbird to a screecher. The nightingale changes its colour and its voice with the seasons; it goes without sleep, devoting itself to song. Some birds do not go hungry in the winter seasons, being fed by the air alone and by the moisture present during their [?]; and they also master the pleasures below the belly. For some mate in spring and in autumn at the equinoxes, and some once a year. Female birds keep to mating until they conceive, and then at once turn away from the males. Beetles die at once if they are smeared with rose oil. Bees and wasps die when soaked in oil, because their pores are blocked. If they are then wetted with vinegar, they revive; for they are sustained by the air, though they do not breathe. Bees have a king. They fly in common and dwell in common, and none of them goes out rashly before the king has begun the flight. Their king is not elected; he holds rule over all by nature, and he differs from them in size, in shape and in gentleness of character. He has a sting, but he does not use it to defend himself. Bees gather wax from the flowers. With their mouths they draw up the moisture scattered like dew on the flowers and put it into the hollows of the wax. That is why it is liquid at first; then, ripened over time, it becomes sweet and useful to people. They also build the storehouses of the honey with wise skill. Stretching the wax into a thin membrane, they build the cells close together and joined to one another, so that the small structure holds together by the binding of its tiniest parts to one another. Locusts encamp across the breadth of the land at a single signal. As they go about they see other crops heavy with grain, yet they do not touch them, but hurry to the place appointed for them, as if driven by a divine command. They do not touch the crop until permission has been given them. Afterwards the seleucis bird is sent against them, and it devours them all, for its nature is insatiable. They say that the owl's sight is dimmed by day and strengthened by night. When bats sleep, they hang from one another, and if one of them happens to be torn from the cluster, the rest cry out. The bat alone among winged creatures is four-legged, and it is furnished with teeth. Cicadas are born in rainy weather, and they are silent at

that season, since they are stiffened by the dew. They say that their wing strikes and sings. On the sixth day God commanded the earth to bring forth four-footed creatures according to their kind, and creeping things, and wild beasts of the earth, and cattle, and all that creep upon the earth according to their kind. At once all these were brought into being. They share sense-perception with man's nature, but they do not possess an equal soul. They live and move with a motion supplied by the primal nature of the blood mixed with the breath of the outside air. Among them too there are various characters that hint at the Providence of God, for these also bear no small witness to it. The wise fruit-bearing of plants, the good order of the stars, the blameless course of the sun and moon, and the law that fixes the bounds of the sea so that it does not overstep them all bear witness to Providence beyond dispute. In the same way the particular nature of the animals, showing an unvarying order, proclaims Providence very clearly, like a soul moving the whole structure of the world. Anyone who rejects it would be ridiculous, since all the elements acknowledge it. The earth does not refuse to grow plants; the sun, the moon and the other stars do not shrink from their proper course; the sea does not overstep the rule it was given; and creatures that swim, fly and walk on land do not fall short of the service they owe. How, then, is anyone who rejects Providence altogether not unjust and senseless? Every argument [?] will say that a work of art does not come about by itself, and that wise works are accomplished by knowledge. When we see a beautifully painted image, we at once form a notion of an artist, and we admire its painter; and when we see a ship skilfully built with knowledge, we praise the shipwright. If we ourselves, seeing works of art, recognize the gifted craftsman, why should we not much rather come to grasp the all-wise Providence of all things, seeing with the mind's eye through the elemental parts of the world, which are arranged with knowledge? For their forms and shapes are enough to make the craftsman known, even if the things composed keep silent and do not speak. Things shaped by someone naturally acknowledge the one who adorned them. Just as the composition of the elements makes Providence plain, so too the varied nature of the animals gives knowledge of it. Anger is born with the lion. Its life is solitary; it shares with none of the animals, and it does not take yesterday's food, only fresh. Its senses are keen: it quickly picks up the scent of hunters and runs off to its cave, sweeping its tracks with its tail so that they are covered with dust and the hunters cannot trace it. Its cub is born blind and is guarded by the lioness for three days. Then the lion comes back from the hunt, breathes into its face, and makes it see and Gen. 1:21, 26.

When it is [?] by a man or by any of the animals, it first lashes itself with its tail, as [the poet says?]: "With its tail it lashes its ribs and haunches on either side, and rouses itself to fight." When it grows old and is too weak to go hunting, it lies in wait near cities, eager to hunt people for its living. Its mouth always smells foul, and it sleeps with its eyelids open. The lioness can barely carry even one cub, for as the cub comes out it tears her womb with the points of its claws. The leopard is impetuous and swift in its attacks, surpassing the others in speed, and it leaps at the faces of the hunters. The bear is sluggish by nature and odd in its ways; its character is deceitful and its body heavy. So when it is often wounded with very deep blows, it heals itself by stuffing the wounds with very dry mullein. When it wrestles, it skilfully tangles its feet with its opponent's, trips him, and seizing him round the middle grips him mightily. The bull is armed with its horns to defend itself against its opponents, and with its feet it dusts itself like an athlete. When the boar sees hunters lying in ambush in the woods, it rises up, but it does not charge until it has whetted its tusks on the nearby trees. There is an animal, the antelope, that is very fierce and hard to hunt. It has long horns like saws, with which it saws through tall, great trees. When it is thirsty it comes to the river Euphrates and [plays with its horns?] among the heather that grows along the river's banks, and it is caught fast by it. For the heather has slender branches, which become tangled around its horns, and it bellows. The hunters hear it, seize it at once, and kill it.
