The deer is timid and sharp-sighted, and hostile to creeping beasts. If a snake escapes it and slips into a crack in a rock, the deer goes, thirsting, to the springs. For it burns so fiercely with thirst that it even puts its tongue out of its mouth

to cool it in the cold air. Then, having filled itself with water, it goes to where the snake is hiding, draws it out of the crack, and tramples it to death. If even a little of its horn or its hair is burned in a house, any beast that may be lurking there runs away. When the deer sheds its horns, it seeks solitude: it takes to an inaccessible cliff and goes after untrodden wilderness, since it has lost its means of defence against the other beasts. Because there are sores at the roots of the shed horns, it goes down [?] into a densely wooded place, so that the wounds will not be sucked by flies, and it grazes at its ease by night. When it has grown its horns again, it boldly comes out even at midday. It wants to test whether its horns have hardened, since while they are tender they break when scorched by the sun. So it puts its head against trees and rubs firmly against them, trying to learn whether the horns are firmly set. Against the bites of venomous spiders it heals itself by eating a crab. If the wild goat on Crete is pierced by an arrow, it eats the plant called dittany and easily heals the wound. Leopards hunt animals with ease. They know well that the other animals delight in their smell, so they settle in deep caves. The animals, as if they had caught the scent of a savoury smell, follow it with their noses; and when they come near the place, the leopards devour them at once. The panther is friendly to all the animals but hostile to the dragon. Its body is spotted with stars, and it is very quiet. As long as it needs no food, it stays asleep in its den. On the third day it comes out hungry and cries with a loud voice, and from its mouth comes a fragrant, spicy scent. The other animals, near and far, are charmed by it and approach, and they follow the panther, delighting in its many-coloured body. The panther goes a little ahead of them, turns back and watches, and whichever animal pleases it, it leaps upon and takes. The elephant is pregnant for a long time, for it ripens the seed for ten years and gives birth only when the offspring has become old. When an elephant falls into a pit and another elephant sees it, that elephant goes and gathers many elephants, and they come and pull the fallen one up, gently lifting it. The dragon in India creeps up over the elephant's back and wraps itself around its whole belly. Whatever vein it happens to cut through, it gorges insatiably on the blood, sucking with violent breath and a fierce hissing. The elephant leaps and [strikes?] its flanks with its trunk, as if the dragon were sitting there. Then, as its blood drains away, it can no longer leap; it stands trembling, and a little later it falls, its legs having given way. Then it dies, and

[as it falls, it?] pins the dragon beneath it. The dragon cannot loosen the coils it had wrapped around the elephant, and, crushed by the elephant's weight, it is choked and dies. The horse is hot in its desire for the female. The donkey is sluggish, sharp of hearing, and has a good memory. The camel bears grudges. The wolf cannot be tamed. The ox is steady. The dog is grateful and loves its master. Often, when masters have been murdered on the road, their dogs have died beside them; others have even exposed the murderers and brought about their just punishment. Some have supposed that the hyena changes each year from female to male, or from male to female. But this is not so. This animal is utterly lascivious, and under its tail, in front of the passage, it has a protrusion resembling the female organ. This has no passage but only a hollow, which serves none of the purposes of a womb and receives only empty lust. Because of their excessive lust, male and female alike have this peculiarity: when their passages are filled and occupied with pregnancy, they practise unnatural intercourse with one another. That is why a female hyena is very rarely found, for this animal is not pregnant continuously. The hare is particularly incontinent in mating. The female gives birth every month, and after giving birth she is mounted again by any hare she happens upon, and she conceives while still nursing; for one is not enough for her. They say the griffin is an enormous creature, so large that it casts a shadow as big as a field. It snatches up a lion as easily as an eagle in our parts snatches a hare. There is an animal, the charadrius, mentioned by Moses. It is very white, and over its whole body it has no spot of any other colour. They say its droppings heal those with dim sight. They report that it lives in royal courts and becomes a prophet of life and death to people who are ill. For when, they say, someone falls ill, they bring the charadrius before him. If it looks at the sick man and the sick man at it, the charadrius swallows his illness, flies up into the sun's upper air, and scatters the man's illness there. If

The ant-lion has a father with the face of a lion and a mother with the face of an ant. The father eats meat and the mother eats pulse, and they beget the ant-lion as a creature of double nature, with the face of a lion and the hind part of an ant. Being able to eat neither meat nor pulse,

The wild ass leads the herd, and it crushes the genitals of the males that are born, so that they cannot breed. The hedgehog's body is like a ball, and its back is covered all over with spines, which are like the spines of sea urchins. It goes to the grape cluster on the vine and knocks down grapes; then it rolls over, spears the grapes on its spines, and goes off. The fox is crafty and hunts birds by the following trick. It finds a muddy pool and rolls in it, then rolls again in very fine dust or chaff. It lays itself out on the plain with its eyes wide open, or holds in its breath, so that it looks bloated and the birds think it is dead. When they fly down onto it, it at once snatches them and devours them. When the lizard grows old it goes blind. It enters a crack in a wall that faces carefully towards the east, and when the sun rises it opens its eyes. Lit by the sun's ray, it [regains its sight?] and is restored to health. So you too, O man, when you have grown old in sins and are blinded in mind, seek the Sun of righteousness, so that you may be renewed in righteousness, gazing on him and seeing again with the eyes of the soul. Of all the beasts the most spirited and the most fiery, and the one that forms itself into the most varied shapes, is the dragon. It coils as it goes, propelling itself forward, and reaches whatever it wants very quickly. It is also long-lived, for it not only sheds old age but also grows even larger. When it has completed its appointed span of life, it is consumed into itself. It does not die by its own end before fulfilling the term of its life, unless someone kills it by force. The ichneumon fights it in single combat, having smeared itself with mud and covering its nostrils with its tail. It also fights the Egyptian asp in the following way. The asp comes at it hissing loudly, dragging its tail in coils, while the front of its body from the chest to the head leaps up into the air. Puffed up, with swollen chest and broad neck, and full of rage, it attacks, flicking its tongue with a fierce hissing. The ichneumon raises its tail and waves it to deceive the asp and draw it on. Crouching on its forelegs, it moves forward, lowering itself completely and stretching out only its face, watching that it does not receive a mortal blow first. When it sees the asp eagerly fighting its tail as though it were a beast, it suddenly leaps on it, squeezes its neck, and strangles it. Patrol. Gr. XVIII.

The lizard called the salamander, if it gets into a furnace or a bath, cools it. They say that the viper receives the male's seed through its mouth, bites off the member itself with its teeth, and kills him. When she becomes pregnant, she in turn is killed by her offspring. While they are still in her belly they eat through the womb, burst the belly, and come out through her side. When the snake grows old it goes blind. It fasts for forty days until its body grows slack, then enters a narrow crack in a rock and, forcing its way through, strips off its old skin and is renewed. When it is thirsty, it first lays aside its venom and only then drinks water from the spring. When it hunts dormice, it blinds them and feeds them, and when they are fattened it eats them. If it sees a man naked, it does not approach him; but if he is clothed,

The basilisk sends out deadly venom from its eye, so that anyone who looks at it dies on the spot. Its breath is fiery and scorches the land and wooded places. They report that it comes into being in this way. When many snakes [are gathered?] together and become pestilent (since the creature is utterly foul), each one devours its neighbour. The strongest snake consumes the weaker ones, and, filled with the venom of all the snakes it has eaten, it becomes a basilisk with a venom so terrible that it kills by its eye alone. The scarab beetle shapes cow dung into a round ball and rolls it while facing backwards. They say that it [lives?] six months above the ground, sows its seed into the ball of dung, and begets a male scarab; for there is never a female scarab. Because of this nature the Egyptians revere it, turning it into a figure of the sun, since it rolls a sphere; and they liken the stars to the shapes of snakes, because the stars travel on a slanting course. When ants gather grain, they cut it through the middle of the kernels, so that it will not sprout when it gets damp. They stay indoors through the winter, having laid up enough food during the summer. The leech is a wormlike creature that lives in fresh water. Someone drinking greedily may swallow it along with the water, for it is so smooth that it slips down with what he drinks. He suffers no small harm from it, as it sucks the blood from his flesh and grows; it is insatiable in its thirst for blood. Often it cannot be drawn out even by doctors who need to remove it, until it bursts. The cat is an enemy of asps and the other biting reptiles. The ibis is the enemy of snakes, locusts and caterpillars. The hawk is deadly to horned vipers, scorpions and the other small reptiles. This creature is

compassionate towards man: if it sees a dead man unburied, it laments and throws earth over him. After making the world, God fashioned man last of all. He broke the cold with the hot and bound the moist with the dry, and again loosened the dry with the moist, and so he put man together, containing all the parts of the universe. The earth, standing firm, holds the cold air poured around it, with fire suspended above it in its ordered place, and water running around it in a circle. In the same way man is like the earth in the solid nature of his bones, and he is made up of the flesh poured over them. He has been given breathing through the nostrils, which, like the air, cools his innate heat. The air above our heads, cooling the fiery nature of the air, makes it temperate for the life of living things. The heat in man's body melts away the excess of phlegm, as it would an icy mass of water. The veins, and the blood in them, are like rivers. When God had fashioned man of this kind from the earth and given him a rational soul, [he placed him in?] the paradise of delight to enjoy it [?] ... Then, when he disobeyed the commandment, God moved him to this very earth and declared that his life on it would be one of toil. Adam knew his wife Eve and begot two sons, Cain and Abel. Cain was a farmer and Abel a shepherd, and the farmer [?] did not seek out the firstfruits of his crops. Abel made an offering to God, and his sacrifice was accepted. Cain first ate his fill of the produce himself and only then made his offering, and his sacrifice was not accepted. Angered at this, Cain killed his brother out of envy. God made him accursed and drove him out of that land. After wandering a long way, he came to a place called Kainan [?] and gave himself to every kind of abomination: he lay in wait for passers-by and killed them, and from the spoils he amassed untold wealth. Cain was the first to devise measures, weights and boundaries of land, and the building of a city, at a time when everyone embraced a pure and untroubled life. Adam stayed in the place where he was and had many sons and daughters. Among them was one outstanding son, Seth. When he came of age, he devised many virtues, and he left his descendants to emulate them. For he was the first to discover astronomy and the whole ordering of the heavens, which Adam arranged to endure until the last times in this way: for when Adam was about to die, he prophesied to his children that God was going to

[?] to wipe out the nature of things in the world by fire and water. When Seth and his people heard this, they made two pillars, building one of stone and the other of baked brick, and on them they engraved the whole movement of the heavens, so that their discovery of astronomy would not be forgotten. If everything were destroyed by water, the stone pillar would survive; if by fire, the brick one. When the deluge came, the stone pillar did survive, and it still stands to this day in the land of Siriad. Cain begot Enoch, Enoch begot Irad, Irad begot Mehujael, Mehujael begot Methushael, and he begot Lamech. Lamech took two wives, Adah and Zillah, and had three sons by them. By Adah he had Jabal, who became a breeder of cattle, and Jubal, who invented the psaltery and the lyre. By Zillah he had Tubal-cain, who became a hammerer of bronze and iron. Adam, having lived nine hundred and twelve years,

Enosh, the son of Seth, hoped to call upon the name of the Lord. He lived nine hundred and five years and died. His son Cainan lived nine hundred and ten years and died. His son Mahalalel lived seven hundred and ninety-five years and died. Mahalalel's son Jared lived nine hundred and sixty years and died. Jared's son Enoch pleased God and was taken away. His son Methuselah lived seven hundred and sixty-nine years and died. Lamech, the son of Methuselah, lived seven hundred and fifty-three years and died. To this Lamech was born a son, Noah, who delighted in the virtues of good deeds and tried to persuade the human race to turn from wickedness to virtue. For until the seventh generation people acknowledged God as master of all things, and of righteousness

But later, as time went on, they ran aground on every kind of lawlessness. Since Noah could not persuade them to give up their wickedness, he came to loathe their company and withdrew to another land. God commanded him to build an ark of four storeys, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide and thirty deep, so that he might shut himself in it together with his family and escape the danger of the flood. For God wished to wipe out the wickedness of the people of that time with such a punishment. When the flood came, the heights of the mountains were covered by the water. Indeed, even now, people cutting building stone on the ridge of Lebanon find kinds of sea fish that happened to be caught in the hollows of the mountains and set hard with the mud.

The ark was lifted up by the water and came to rest on a peak of a mountain in Armenia. When the water subsided, everyone in the ark went out. The local people still call that place the Place of Disembarkation; they point out the remains of the ark and use its bitumen to ward off evil. Noah died, having lived nine hundred and fifty years. His sons persuaded all the others, who were afraid to move from the mountain (for they suspected they would suffer another deluge), to come down and settle the broad plain. So that they would not multiply and then start feuding with one another, God commanded them to found colonies. But they did not obey, because they were farming good land and had a great abundance of crops. So he again struck them with a grievous misfortune, to make them send out colonies. Even so they did not yield to God's will, but supposed that the fertility of the land came to them not by God's kindness but by their own strength. It was Nimrod the giant who persuaded them to hold this conceit, a daring man and mighty in combat. He turned them away from God and compelled them to pay reverence to himself instead, and he set them to building a tower that would touch the height of heaven, threatening to take revenge on God if he brought a flood on the world again. As the multitude zealously joined him in this madness and built the tower faster than words can tell, God at once confused their speech, and because of the difference of tongues they were scattered. For this reason the place took the name Babylon, since the Hebrews call confusion "Babel." Each group occupied whatever land it came upon, and they filled the whole coastland and the mainland, and the islands as well, for they crossed the sea in ships and put in at them. Some of the nations keep the names of those who founded them, while others have changed them, because the Greeks later conquered them and embellished the nations with their own names. They also laid down laws of their own for them, so as to claim for themselves the glory of founding them and leave later generations no suspicion that others had come first. Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. [?] Beginning from the Taurus and Amanus mountains, they settled and advanced in Asia as far as the river Tanais, and in Europe as far as Gadeira. They are these: Gomer, who founded the Gomareans, now the Galatians; Magog, the Magogians, now the Scythians; Madai, the Madaeans, now the Medes; Javan, Ionia and the Greeks; [?] Tubal, the Thobelians, now the Iberians; Meshech, the Meschenians, now the [?].

[?] and the Lebanon mountains they occupied the land, seizing all that faced toward the sea [?], and appropriating the lands as far as the Ocean. For some of these the names have been changed altogether; for others they have been altered into forms hard to recognize; and only a few still keep their names intact. The sons of Ham are these: Cush, from whom come the Cushites, now the Ethiopians; Mizraim, from whom come the Mestraeans, now the Egyptians; Put, the Putites, now the Libyans, and to this day the river among the Moors and the region near it are called [?]. The nation and the country came to be called Libyan after one of the sons of Mizraim, named Libys, who reigned over them. Cush had seven sons: Seba, from whom come the Sabaeans, who to this day keep the name together with their land; Havilah, from whom come the Evilaeans, now the Gaetulians; Sabtah, from whom come the Sabathenes, now the Astabari; Raamah, from whom come the Allaeans, who still bear this name today; Judadan, from whom come the Judadaeans, an Ethiopian nation that to this day bears the same name as its forefather; Sabteca, from whom come the Sabactenes, who likewise bear his name. [?] This Nimrod stayed in Babylon and was the first to rule them as a tyrant. Mizraim had eight sons, who occupied the land from Gaza as far as Egypt. The land of Philistim kept that name for a time, but was later called Palestine. Canaan too had eleven children. Sidon, the firstborn, founded a city in Phoenicia named Sidon after himself. Hamathaeus built Hamath, now Epiphania, after a famous Macedonian took control of it and gave it his own name. Arucaeus founded a territory in Lebanon. Aradius [?] the island of Arados. Asenassus, from whom come the Asennaeans. Samaraeus founded Samaria; the Hittite founded the Hittites; the Jebusite founded the Jebusites; the Amorite founded the Amorites, who lived in Bethel; the Girgashite founded the Girgashites, who lived beyond the Jordan as far as Philadelphia; the Hivite founded the Hivites. The Kenites lived around Lebanon and Amarus [?]; the Anakim giants lived in Hebron, and around it the Hittites and the

Perizzites, mingled with the Canaanites, held Palestine; others held Raphia [?] Philadelphia. The Girgashites, again, held Gadara and the city of Gergesa, and the Lake of Tiberias; and the Jebusites held what is now Jerusalem. Shem too had five sons, who settled Asia as far as the Indian [?] Ocean, starting from the Euphrates. They are these: Elam, from whom come the Elamites, now the Persians; Asshur, from whom come the Assyrians; Arphaxad, from whom come the Arphaxaeans, now the Chaldeans; Aram, from whom come the Aramaeans, now the Syrians. These held the land from Mesopotamia as far as the mountains of Ararat, which lie toward Armenia. Lud, from whom come the Lydaeans, now the Lydians; Cainan, from whom come the Canatae [?]. Aram had four sons: Uz, who founded Damascus and Trachonitis, which lies between Palestine and Coele-Syria; Hul [?], from whom come the Lazoneis; Gether, from whom come the Staphenians [?]; Mash, from whom come the Massenians. The son of Arphaxad was Cainan, from whom come the Sogdians; he was also the one who invented astronomy and augury. Cainan had a son, Shelah, from whom come the Susianians. Shelah's son was Eber, from whom come the Hebrews, who kept the ancient Hebrew language, because Eber had not taken part in building the tower and so did not have his speech changed. The sons of Eber were Peleg, from whom come the Adiabenians, and Joktan, from whom come the Hebramaeans [?]. Peleg was so called because he was born at the time the colonies were sent out; for the Hebrews call a division "Peleg," since in his time they were divided. And the number of years the world is thought to last was then divided into two exactly equal parts, for three thousand years had been completed since the world came into being. For we reckon that creation will last until the sixth millennium, since God completed this universe in six days. I think that the Divine reckons days as a thousand years each, for, it says, "a day of the Lord is as a thousand years." So from Adam to the death of Peleg there are three thousand years, and to the coming and resurrection of the Lord five thousand five hundred and thirty-one years, so that four hundred and fifty-nine years of the sixth millennium remain. The Sabbath is a sign of the consummation of the world. And it is fitting that the Lord, who came to dwell in the world in the last days, suffered on the Day of Preparation, which is the sixth day, and that it was about the sixth hour of that day when he was crucified; by this Scripture signifies the half of the sixth millennium. That is why it did not say precisely "the sixth hour": Scripture was hinting that the number is exceeded by a little. From Christ to the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine

there are [?] years. Just as Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster and was given back unharmed, so we too, all of us, after passing through the three spans of the age on earth, shall rise again. For time has three universal spans: present, past and future. Our Saviour arranged symbols of these by spending three days and three nights in the earth, clearly teaching that when these spans of time have been completed, our resurrection will take place, which is the beginning of the age to come. Joktan had these sons: Almodad, from whom come the Indians; Sheleph, from whom come the Bactrians; Hazarmaveth, from whom come the Arabs; Jerah, from whom come the Carmanians; Hadoram, from whom come the Mardi; Uzal, from whom come the Arians; Diklah, from whom come the Gedrosians; Ebal, from whom come the Scythians; Abimael, from whom come the Hyrcanians; Sheba, from whom come the Arabs of Arabia Felix; Ophir, from whom come the Armenians; Havilah, from whom come the gymnosophists. All these are sons of Shem. Shelah begot Reu; Reu begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor and taught him the divination and astronomy of the Chaldeans. In the time of Serug the sons of Noah began to worship idols and to practise every kind of wickedness, to build cities, set up kings, besiege, plunder and take captives. Nahor begot Terah, and Terah begot Abraham, Nahor and Haran. Haran begot Lot, Sarah and Milcah. Haran died in a city of the Chaldeans called Ur, where his tomb is still shown today. He died in the fire with which Abram burned his father's idols, when he went in to rescue them. They married the sisters: Nahor married Milcah, and Abraham married Sarah. They did not do this unlawfully, since there had never yet been a law forbidding it. For if nature, summoning them to have children, necessarily led the males and females born of Adam, the common father of all, and of his wife, who were brothers and sisters, so that brothers entered into marriage with sisters, then it is not surprising that those who came after, belonging to the first line of descent, followed the law of their forebears. Terah, hating Chaldea because of his grief for his son, moved to Mesopotamia and died there at the age of two hundred and five. From that time on human life was cut short and became briefer, down to the birth of Moses. For after Moses the limit of life became one hundred and twenty years, which Moses himself lived before [ending] his mortal life
Abraham the thrice-blessed was an excellent astronomer and wiser than the others in virtue. When all the sons of Noah had [?] into superstition

he alone declared that God is the Creator of all things, inferring this from the changes that affect the sun and the moon and from what happens to the earth, the air and the sea. "For why," he says, "if they had in themselves the power to keep their own good order, do they not take care of it, but fall short of it?" From this, then, one can see that each of them does its work not by its own power, even though it seems to benefit people greatly, but by the will of the one who made it. The Chaldeans and the people of Mesopotamia quarrelled with him over this opinion and opposed him. So he left that place and, at God's command, settled in the land of the Canaanites. When a terrible famine struck, he went to Egypt. The Egyptians held opinions opposed to one another and scorned and overturned one another's customs, and he showed that none of them thought or taught anything of value. Admired for his intelligence and great wisdom, he handed on to them arithmetic and astronomy; before his arrival the Egyptians knew nothing of these, and after learning them they later passed them on to the Greeks. When Abraham returned from Egypt, a son, Ishmael, was born to him by his slave girl Hagar, from whom the nation of the Hagarenes and Saracens arose, while the nation of the Ishmaelites came from Ishmael. Lot parted from Abraham and settled in the region of Sodom, which was condemned to be burned by fire from heaven for its lawless transgression, and even now its burnt traces can be seen. For one can see the shadows of five cities, in which a fruit grows that looks from the outside like edible fruit, but when taken in the hands dissolves into ash and smoke. Next to this region lies the Asphalt Lake. It was formerly a valley with wells of bitumen, but when the region was destroyed it became a lake, which is also called the Dead Sea. It is extremely bitter by nature and barren, but its water is so buoyant that heavy objects thrown into it, stone or iron, may not sink to the bottom but are blown back up as if by a breath and float on the surface. Living people thrown into it bob back up, while the dead sink; lit lamps float, but once extinguished they sink. It throws up bitter salt, alum and black lumps of bitumen as big as headless bulls. Sailors grab these lumps, fill their boats with them and haul them to the shore. The bitumen sticks fast to the wood of the boat and cannot be removed in any way unless it is wetted with urine and women's menstrual blood, for these are the only things it naturally yields to. They also say that the water changes colour three times a day and gives off a varied appearance when the sun's rays shine on it. Abraham, at a hundred years of age, begot a legitimate

son by Sarah, Isaac, and circumcised him after the eighth day. From this the Hebrews keep the custom even now, being circumcised on that day. The Arabs and the Ishmaelites, on the other hand, are circumcised in their thirteenth year, since their forefather Ishmael was circumcised at that age. At Sarah's urging, Abraham sent Ishmael away somewhere else, so that after his own death Ishmael would not, as the firstborn, wrong Isaac over the birthright. The descendants of Ishmael occupied the land stretching from the Euphrates to the Red Sea. Some time later God commanded Isaac to be offered to him as a sacrifice. Abraham, considering this too the greatest token of piety, went with great eagerness to a mountain peak, and when he had prepared everything for the sacrifice, he said to his son: "My child, I asked God with countless prayers that you might be born to me, and once you came into the world there was nothing I did not spare in bringing you up, nor anything in which I thought I would be happier than to see you grown to manhood and to leave you at my death as the heir of my rule. But since it was by God's will that I became your father, I now give you back to him at his request. So bear this consecration nobly. For I yield you to God, who has thought us worthy of this honour, in return for the kindness and protection he has shown me. Go, then, not dying the common way people leave this life, but sent ahead by your own father to God, the Father of all, by the rite of sacrifice. I think he has judged you worthy to be taken not by disease, nor by war, nor by any of the other sufferings that naturally befall people, but to have your soul received by him with prayers and holy rites. And in your place you will provide me with God as guardian and comfort of my old age." When Isaac heard this he said to him: "I would not have deserved to be born at all if I were going to reject the decision of God and of my father and not readily give myself up to the will of both. Even if my father alone had chosen this, it would be wrong not to obey." And saying this he hurried to the altar, and

he took Rebecca in marriage, by whom he had two sons, Esau and Jacob. After Sarah died, Abraham married Keturah and had six sons by her: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. These too had children: Shuah had Sheba and Dedan, and from Dedan came Letushim, Asshurim and Leummim; Midian had Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah. For all of these Abraham devised [?], and they took Troglodytis and parts of Arabia Felix, as far as it reaches the Red Sea. Assyria was named after Asshurim. Sophren campaigned against Libya and took possession of it, and his descendants, that is, the grandsons who settled there, called the country Africa after his name. They fought as allies of Heracles when he campaigned against Antaeus the earth-born. Heracles married the daughter of [?], by whom he had a son [?], who begot a son, Sophon, after whom the barbarians are called Sophones. Abraham died at the age of one hundred and seventy-five. Jacob, having stolen Esau's blessing, went to Mesopotamia to Laban, his mother's brother. He served him fourteen years and married his two daughters, Leah and Rachel, the one he desired more. He did not desire her because he was overcome by her beauty (although, as it is written, Rachel was beautiful in form and very lovely to look at), but because she was the first person he saw and she met him as if by divine providence, so he embraced her and loved her. He knew that this same marvel had happened in the case of his mother Rebecca, when Abraham's servant prayed and things turned out for him as he had prayed, and what he had set out to do was fulfilled in deeds. Leah bore him six sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun; Rachel bore Joseph and Benjamin; Rachel's slave girl Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali; and Leah's slave girl, named Zilpah, bore Gad and Asher. The nation of the Syrians arose from Esau. They were also called Idumaeans, because Esau was earlier called Idumaeus, since he had craved the red [?]; for the Hebrews call red "Edom." Later they were renamed Syrians after a certain Syrus who ruled their nation. Esau took three wives from among the Canaanites: Adah, the daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah the Hebrew; and Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth. By Adah he begot Eliphaz, by Basemath Reuel, and by Oholibamah Jeush, Jalam and Korah. After fathering these in the land of the Canaanites, he moved to Mount Seir, because he could not [?] his brother Jacob

…when he returned from Mesopotamia, to live together because of the great number of their possessions. So he had a son there too, and named him Edom after his own surname. His sons also had legitimate children: to Eliphaz were born five, Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz, among whom there was also a bastard, Amalek, born to him in turn by a concubine named Timna. To Reuel likewise four sons were born, Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah; and to Edom eleven: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel and Zephonen. To Seir the Horite, who settled in the land of Lotan, five sons were born: Shobal, Zibeon, [?], Asher and Reson; and to Lotan two, Hori and Heman. Timna was the sister of Lotan, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. Shobal the son of Seir had five children: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam; and Zibeon two, [?] and Anah, who found the Iamin in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of his father Zibeon. [Anah] fathered Dishon and a daughter, Oholibamah; and Dishon fathered Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran. Asher, the fourth son of Seir, fathered four children: Balam, Zoukam, Ioukam and Oukam; and Oreson, the fifth son of Seir, fathered Ossaran. Before kings reigned in Israel, these kings reigned over Edom: Balak son of Beor, and the name of his city was Dennaba; after him Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah; after him Hushan from the land of the Temanites; after him [Hadad] son of Bedad, who cut down Midian in the plain of Moab, and the name of his city was Gittaim; after him Samlah from Masrekah; after him Saul from Rehoboth by the river; after him Baal-hanan son of Achbor, who had a wife named Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, son of Mezahab. All of these together reigned [?] years. Now the sons of Jacob, hating their brother Joseph out of envy, sold him to the Ishmaelites, and these sold him into Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh's chief cook. At this time Judah went to a certain Hirah, an Adullamite; and there he saw a Canaanite woman named Shua, took her in marriage, and had four children by her: Er, [Onan], Shelah and Perez. Judah took for his firstborn son Er a wife named Tamar, and because of the great wickedness of his ways Er died childless, God having put him to death. Then Judah charged his second son Onan to lie with Tamar, so as to raise up offspring for his brother. But Onan, knowing that the sowing of children would not count as his, spilled his seed on the ground whenever he was about to lie with the woman; and God, angered at this, struck him dead at once. So Judah ordered Tamar to remain a widow in her father's house until Shelah should grow up. But when he had reached manhood Judah was afraid to join him to Tamar, suspecting that he too might perish. She was bitterly grieved at this, and paid Judah back by [?] means. When he came

to the shearing of the sheep, she heard of it, took off her mourning clothes, put on costly garments, and sat at the gates of the city of Enaim. Judah, passing by there, saw her and desired her as a harlot, for she had veiled her face so as not to be recognized; and promising to send her a kid, he asked to lie with her. But she did not yield until she had received his ring, his cord and his staff as a pledge. When he had lain with her, he went off to his flocks, while she changed back into her widow's clothes and stayed hidden out of sight. When Judah sent the kid and tried to get back the cord and the rest, and could not find her, he was galled at having been tricked; yet he held his peace, though he wanted by every means to uncover the deceit. After some time Tamar was found to be pregnant, and when Judah heard that she had conceived by harlotry, he ordered her to be burned alive. As she was being led out, she sent Judah the cord, the ring and the staff, saying, "I have conceived by the man to whom these belong. Recognize, then, whose ring, cord and staff these are." Judah was dismayed at the matter, and coming to himself he blamed himself for the wrong, saying, "She is more in the right than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah." When her time came, she gave birth to twins. The elder, that is, the first, put his hand out first, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one will come out first." But at once the child drew his hand back inside, and his brother came out first, and his name was called Perez; and after him came out his brother, who had the scarlet on his hand, and he was named Zerah. From these was descended Joseph, the betrothed of the immaculate Mary, from whom Christ took flesh. For, as the evangelist Matthew records, Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, Obed fathered Jesse, Jesse fathered David the king, and David the king fathered Solomon by the wife of Uriah, Solomon fathered Rehoboam, Rehoboam fathered Abijah, Abijah fathered Asa, Asa fathered Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat fathered Joram, Joram fathered Uzziah, Uzziah fathered Jotham, Jotham fathered Hezekiah, Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, Manasseh fathered Amon, Amon fathered Josiah, Josiah fathered Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon; and after the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah fathered Shealtiel, Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel, Zerubbabel fathered

Abiud, Abiud fathered Eliakim, Eliakim fathered Azor, Azor fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Achim, Achim fathered Eliud, Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, Matthan fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ. So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ fourteen generations. We must now ask on what account Matthew and Luke disagree in the genealogy of Joseph, the one writing that he was the son of Jacob the son of Matthan, while Luke writes that he was the son of Heli the son of Melchi; and how these two, Melchi and Matthan, who were of different lines, both turn out to be grandfathers of Joseph. The matter is explained as follows. First Matthan, of the line of Solomon, took a wife named Estha [?], fathered Jacob by her, and died. Then Melchi, of the line of [?], took her and had Heli by her. So, since Matthan and Melchi married the same woman, they fathered two brothers by the same mother; and for this reason we find Jacob and Heli belonging to two different lines. Heli took a wife and died childless, and his brother Jacob took his wife so as to raise up children for his brother according to the law, and fathered Joseph by her. Thus Joseph was by nature the son of Jacob, but by law

It is also worth going through the account that a certain James relates about holy Mary. He says that among the tribes of Israel there was a rich man named Joachim, who at each feast brought gifts to God twice as large as those of others, saying, "What comes from my abundance shall be for all the people, and what is for forgiveness shall be for my atonement before the Lord God." Now when the great feast of the Lord came round, and everyone was bringing gifts to God as usual, he made to offer first. But a certain Reuben prevented him from offering first, saying that he had no right to, since he was childless in Israel. Grieved at this, he went into the wilderness, pitched a tent there, and begged God to grant him too, as he had granted Abraham, the offspring of a child of his own; for he [?] that he alone was such in Israel; and he went on entreating God, fasting for forty days. In the same way his wife too put on mean clothing and prayed to God that she might have a child. But when the great day of God arrived, she put on a splendid robe, for it was not lawful to wear mourning dress at that feast. About the ninth hour of the day she sat down under a tree in her garden and prayed to God, saying, "God of our fathers, bless me and hear my prayer, as you blessed the womb of Sarah and gave her a son, Isaac." As she said this she looked up into the tree, and seeing a sparrow tending its young,

she groaned bitterly and wailed, saying, "Alas, Lord, that I am not even like these birds, which are fruitful!" As she was crying this out to God, an angel of the Lord appeared to her and announced to her the good news that she would bear a child. When she heard it, she promised at once to dedicate the child to God. The angel made the same things known to Joachim on the mountain. Coming down from the mountain, Joachim offered the Lord a sacrifice of ten ewe lambs, twelve calves to the priests, and a hundred goats to the elders and all the people. Having completed these sacrifices in the temple of God, he came home; and he knew his wife, and had a daughter by her, and named her Mariam. When she was three years old they consecrated her to the temple of God. When she was twelve, the priests held a council as to whom they should give her in marriage. They charged the high priest Zacharias to enter the Holy of Holies and ask God to reveal to him to whom she ought to be joined. While Zacharias was praying, an angel appeared and instructed him to gather all the widowers among the people, each holding a rod; and to whomever God should show a sign, to him he should join the virgin. Zacharias went out and did as the angel had commanded him. Taking all their rods, he went into the sanctuary and prayed, and coming out he gave each man back his own rod. When he handed the last rod to Joseph, a great sign took place: the moment he received his rod from the priest, a dove flew out of the rod and settled on Joseph's head. The high priest and all the priests with him, marvelling at what had happened, judged that he should become the betrothed of the girl. Joseph took her and kept her in his care; and leaving her in his house he went off to finish his building work, for he was a carpenter by trade. At that time the priests decided that a veil for the temple of God should be made by pure virgins, and seven virgins were found in the tribe of Judah. Zacharias, remembering Mary, ordered her also to be included in the number; and bringing them into the house of God, he ordered them to cast lots to see which should spin the gold, the undefiled, the fine linen, the silk, the true purple, the blue and the scarlet; and the lot fell to Mary to work the purple and the scarlet. While she was working at home, an angel appeared and announced to her the wondrous birth, as the Gospels relate. When she had finished the work assigned to her, she gave it to the high priest, and having been blessed by him she went away; and after a time she gave birth to Christ according to the flesh. When the magi from the East worshipped him as a king and brought him gifts, Herod was troubled and planned to kill him at once. But he was carried off into Egypt by Joseph and Mary, and so escaped the death

intended by Herod. Herod, not knowing of the flight, ordered all the children in Bethlehem to be killed, and among them he was eager to kill John too, who was still an infant. But Elizabeth snatched him up and fled into the wilderness; and when she prayed, the mountain split open and received her with the child, and an angel of God guarded them. So Herod sent to Zacharias: "Hand over your son; tell me where you have hidden him." Zacharias sent back word to him, saying, "I am always in attendance at the altar; I do not know what has become of my son." Herod was angered and sent to him again, saying, "Hand over your son. Do you not know that your blood is in my hand?" And Zacharias said, "I am a martyr of God. You may have my blood, but God will receive my spirit. Know, however, that you are shedding innocent blood at the threshold of the temple of the Lord." Herod, enraged at this, ordered him to be killed beside the altar before daybreak, so that the people should not prevent his murder. At dawn the priests came to the temple and were puzzled that the high priest did not come to meet them as usual, and they waited outside. As time went on, one of them ventured to go in. He saw blood congealed beside the altar and heard a voice saying, "Zacharias has been murdered, and his blood will not be wiped away until the avenger comes." Hearing this he was terrified, and went out and told the priests. They went in and did not see the body, only the blood; and tearing their robes they beat their breasts in mourning, and told the people, and lamented him for three days and nights. After this they appointed by lot Simeon to his office, who had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord's Christ. Another story about Zacharias is also current: that there was a place in the temple where only virgins were allowed to enter and worship God, while it was not lawful for married women to do so. Now Mary, after giving birth to the Saviour, came and stood in this place. When those who knew she had given birth tried to stop her, Zacharias said that she was worthy of the place of the virgins. So, as one who had broken the law regarding the place of the virgins, they killed him beside the altar. But these things have been said in passing. Joseph, having been sold into Egypt by his brothers, interpreted Pharaoh's dreams by divine insight and was made ruler of all Egypt. When famine was pressing hard on the whole land, his brothers went down into Egypt, they too, to buy grain because of the famine; and Joseph made himself known to them and [sent for]

them, together with their father Jacob, to come into Egypt with their whole household. To Reuben four sons had been born: Enoch, Phallu, Hezron and Carmi; to Simeon six: Jemuel, Jamin, [?], Achi, Zohar and Saul; to Levi three: Gershon, Kohath and Merari; to Judah five: Er and Onan, who died as was written above, Shelah, Perez and Zerah; to Perez two, Hezron and Hamul; to Issachar four: Tola, Puah, Jashub and Shimron; to Zebulun three: Sered, Elon and Jahleel. All these, thirty-three in number, were descended from Leah, along with a daughter, Dinah. To Gad were born seven sons: Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi and Areli; to Asher four: Imnah, Ishvah, Beriah, and Serah a daughter; and from Beriah were born Heber and Malchiel. All these, sixteen in number, were sons of Zilpah, Leah's maid, who bore them to Jacob in Leah's name. To Joseph two sons were born in Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphera of Heliopolis, bore him. From Manasseh was born Machir, by a concubine who was a Syrian by race, and Machir fathered Gilead; from Ephraim were born sons, Shuthelah, Bad and Lam; and from Shuthelah was born Eden. To Benjamin likewise two children were born, Ballachobor and Ashbel; and from Ballachobor, Gera, Naaman, Laches, Hezron and Muppim; and Muppim fathered Ard. These were the sons of Rachel, eighteen in all. [?] was born to Dan; and to Naphtali, Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem. These were the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's maid, seven in all. The blessed Jacob, having lived 147 years in all, died in Egypt, after first blessing each of his sons with different blessings. He gave the blessing of the firstborn to Joseph and not to Reuben, because Joseph, by not yielding to the pleasure offered by the Egyptian woman, was justified, whereas Reuben was overcome and sinned; and besides, Joseph was the firstborn of Rachel. He assigned the kingship to the tribe of Judah and not to that of Reuben, because, while Judah was disgraced over a woman, he was justified when he candidly confessed that he himself, and not the woman, was guilty of the sin. He was also appointed to reign for this reason, that his tribe alone of all the tribes was the boldest in zeal for God and in avenging him; and therefore Jacob prophesies that Christ will spring from him according to [the flesh]. To Levi alone he assigned the high priesthood, because Amram, who sprang from him, defied Pharaoh's decree and kept his son Moses alive. And Reuben alone he made great in number, because he did not consent to the plot against Joseph. When Jacob died in Egypt, they carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him there, and likewise all his sons. Finally, when they departed from Egypt, they buried Joseph too where their forefather Abraham had been

buried. In that place stood the terebinth under which Jacob hid Laban's idols, which even now is venerated by the people living nearby in honour of their ancestors; for to this day there is an altar beside its trunk, on which they used to offer burnt offerings and hecatombs. They say it was the staff of one of the angels who were Abraham's guests, which he planted in the place while he was there, and from it grew this wondrous terebinth. When it is set alight, the whole tree becomes fire, and everyone thinks it is being reduced to ash by the flame; yet once the fire is put out, it is shown to be whole and undamaged. After Joseph's death the Egyptians, forgetting his benefactions, subjected the race of the Israelites to all kinds of hardships, being filled with envy and jealousy toward them. For the Israelites, being hardy in labour, surpassed the Egyptians in virtue and in wealth, while the Egyptians had grown slack through drunkenness and idleness and were forever shackled by sloth. One of the sacred scribes among the Egyptians foretold to Pharaoh that someone would be born among the Israelites who would humble all Egypt and raise his own nation to a great height of prosperity, winning glory that would be remembered for ever. For this reason Pharaoh was determined to destroy the Hebrews by every means. He laid on them heavy labours, ordering them to wall all the cities of Egypt, to cut the river into many canals, and to raise embankments so that the river would in no way flood and damage the city; besides this, to raise pyramids. And he decreed that the babies born among them should be thrown into the river, thinking that he would also destroy in the river the one who had been foretold to overthrow Egypt. Now there was a man of the tribe of Levi named Amram, who married Jochebed and by her fathered the divinely inspired Moses, and he kept him hidden for some time. But when he saw the king's law being enforced more harshly, fearing that he would be caught, he put the child in a basket and set it out on the banks of the river. Pharaoh's daughter, coming there to bathe, saw the basket and opened it, and delighted by the child's beauty she adopted him, since she had no child of her own. She summoned many Egyptian nurses, but could not find a way to rear the child, for he would not take the breast of any of them. At last his mother, secretly presented to the princess, was appointed to nurse him; for he accepted her breast alone, embracing, I think, from his very swaddling clothes his own people and loathing the foreign. When he had grown up, Thermuthis (for that was the princess's name) called him Moses, because he had been saved from the water; for the Egyptians call water [?] and being saved "ses." Before this his parents had called him Melchi. He was so very handsome in appearance that anyone who met him on the road would stand aside in amazement

[?] and marveling greatly at his beauty. So when he had grown, Thermuthis brought him to her father, asking him to make the boy the successor to his kingdom, and she placed him in his arms. The king took him, pressed him to his breast and kissed him. In play he took the diadem from his own head and set it on the boy's head. But Moses threw the diadem to the ground and trampled on it. The scribe who had foretold his birth saw this and understood that this was the one prophesied to be the enemy of the Egyptians' rule. He rushed to kill him but could not; and crying out he said to the king: "This is the one, O king, who the deity foretold to us would spring up from the Hebrews to plot against the kingdom of the Egyptians. Even now he has given no small sign of what is to come, by throwing down the very emblem of the kingship and trampling it into the ground. So if you kill him, you will rid the Egyptians of the evils they expect, and you will make the Hebrews fail of the hope they have in him." When he had said this, the king, by the providence of God, shrank from the murder; and Thermuthis snatched Moses out of the king's hands and kept him safe. Now the Ethiopians, who were neighbors of the Egyptians, suddenly invaded and besieged Egypt. They routed the Egyptians who were drawn up against them and advanced as far as Memphis and the sea, until the Egyptians, following an oracle, took the Hebrew nation as their ally and went out against them. Then Pharaoh, thinking he had found a fitting opportunity to do away with Moses, asked Thermuthis to hand Moses over to him so that he might make him general of the Hebrews. He swore that he would do him no harm, but only appoint him commander of the Hebrews, supposing that he would easily be killed by the enemy, since he had no experience of battle. She first reproached her father and the scribes at length, because the one they had wanted to kill as an enemy they were now calling upon as a helper; then she gave Moses to them. Having been put forward as general of his own people, Moses led the army secretly from the Ethiopians by another road, one that was waterless and teeming with wild beasts (for it breeds every kind of beast, so that some in it even fly). So that no one would be struck by the beasts, he ordered each man to carry woven baskets filled with ibises, for this creature is hostile to asps. So as they passed through that place they let the ibises loose on the beasts, and the beasts, unable to withstand their attack, were destroyed. Having passed through in this way, he suddenly fell upon the Ethiopians, slaughtered a great multitude of them, and put the rest to flight.

The Ethiopians, having barely escaped slaughter by fleeing, reached the city of Saba. This was their royal city, fortified with a strong wall and earthworks, and inaccessible because of the Nile (since the river encircles the whole city with its stream); for this reason it was also hard

for the Egyptians to besiege. So Moses brought the army up to the city, though he was at a complete loss, because it was so hard to capture. While the Egyptians were devising many schemes and achieving nothing, the king's daughter, named Tharmeis, saw Moses from the towers. Delighted by his beauty and admiring the ingenuity of his attempts, she fell in love with him; and she sent the most trusted of her servants to speak with him about marriage. Moses promised to do this if she would hand the city over to him. She at once made peace and handed the city over to him. So when the fighting was ended and the Egyptians had returned to their own places, he took her in marriage; and he founded a city and named it Hermopolis, for this is what the Egyptians call Moses, because he produced the interpretation of the sacred writings. He was also honored not a little among the Ethiopians for his admirable wisdom. For he was the first to devise for them the use of [?], and machines for setting stones, and Egyptian weapons, and instruments for drawing water and for war. Moreover, he divided all Egypt into thirty nomes in order to secure the kingdom for Chenephres, since the Egyptians had been ruled without order, setting up and deposing whomever they chose at will. For these reasons he was honored by the priests as a god and by the Ethiopians as a king; and indeed they learned circumcision from him and keep it to this day. For he was the first wise man, as Eupolemus relates, and was the first to hand down letters to the Hebrews, which the blessed Abraham had brought from the Chaldeans; for the Chaldeans were the first inventors of them. The Phoenicians received them from the Hebrews, and Cadmus carried them over to the Greeks. After the campaign against the Ethiopians Moses came to Egypt. Chenephres welcomed him with fair words, but in deed was plotting his death. Having cut him off from his kinsmen, he went with him to Memphis and asked him what was useful to men. He said: "The race of oxen, because by them the land is made fit for plowing." So Chenephres ordered the people to build a sanctuary for the bull Apis, and he buried under the floor of the temple the memorials of Moses' excellence (these were made of bronze and proclaimed the device of the ibises and the story of his valor against the Ethiopians), so as to consign his deeds to oblivion. The crowd of Hebrews who attended him he divided between two tasks: some he sent out to guard Ethiopia, and others he charged to build the temple in Diospolis of stone, quarrying the nearby mountain, for the temple had formerly been built of baked brick. Having also turned the Egyptians against him, he commanded his friends to kill him, making them all swear not to reveal to him the plot being contrived against him. When all of them refused this scheme, a certain Chanethothes agreed to serve the king's purpose, promising to murder Moses by treachery. Then, when

Merrhoe (for this is what Thermuthis was called) died, Pharaoh, regarding the occasion as a godsend, ordered Moses and Chanethothes to bury her in the regions beyond Egypt. As they were on their way, one of those who knew Pharaoh's intention disclosed it to Moses. Moses guarded himself on every side and buried Merrhoe, and he named both the place and the river Meroe after her. Then he crossed the Nile from Memphis and, at the suggestion of his brother Aaron, fled into Arabia. When Chanethothes learned of this, he drew his sword and went to meet him; but Moses seized his hand, wrenched the sword from his grasp, and killed him with his own sword. He came into Arabia to Raguel, the ruler of those parts, and taking his daughter Sepphora in marriage he fathered two sons by her. Pharaoh, learning of all that Moses had done, poured out his anger on the multitude of the Jews and ordered them to be utterly destroyed. He commanded that they alone should wear linen clothing, so that they would be easily recognized, and so handed them over to the Egyptians for slaughter. For this God punished him with the severest penalty: Pharaoh became the first of all men to contract elephantiasis, and ended his life in a shameful death. The one who succeeded him in the same rule of the kingdom was also the successor to his wickedness, for he subjected the Jews to the same evils. And when great lamentation surrounded them, God took pity on them and sent Moses into Egypt, commanding Pharaoh to release the nation of the Jews into the desert, so that they might worship

Angered at these words of Moses, Pharaoh ordered him to be thrown into prison at once. During the night the whole land was shaken by an earthquake, so that some of the guards died of fright, while the limbs of others went slack in deep sleep. The very gates of the prison flew open, and Moses went out and came by night to the palace; for its doors too had come apart as the earth shook. While all the bodyguards slept, he woke Pharaoh, saying: "God has sent me, commanding you to release the people of the Jews." Pharaoh, astonished, asked who he was and what was the name of the God who had sent him. Moses bent down to his ear and declared to him the name of God; and Pharaoh, unable to bear the hearing of it, fell speechless to the ground. Moses came and raised him up; and he engraved the all-seeing name on a tablet and sealed it. One of the Egyptian priests who dared to scorn this name at once ended his life in convulsions. Pharaoh told Moses to perform some sign; and Moses threw the rod he was holding onto the ground and changed it into a serpent, and taking hold of it again he restored it to its former state.

When even at this Pharaoh would not give way and release the people, Moses prayed to God, and a great earthquake with hail burst upon them, so that whoever fled out of the houses to escape the earthquake was killed by the hail, while those who hurried to avoid the hail were crushed by the earthquake. When he remained unmoved even at this, Moses struck the water of the Nile with the rod, and the river flooded Egypt and very nearly inundated all of it, so that from that time until now it has made its yearly descent. Pharaoh then summoned the priests of the region above Memphis and threatened to wipe out both them and all the shrines of the idols unless they worked wonders like those of Moses. They used their accustomed sorceries to make serpents crawl out and changed the color of the river in appearance, so that Pharaoh, puffed up by this, subjected the Jews to the severest punishment. Then Moses struck the earth with his rod and caused a winged creature to crawl out of it, which settled on the bodies of the Egyptians and gave them painful sores, so that medicine could bring them no help. When Pharaoh was hardened even at this plague, Moses finally brought death upon the firstborn of all Egypt. And when boundless mourning seized Egypt at this, Pharaoh sent all the Jews, with all their families, out of the country. They covered a long road, crossed the rivers of Arabia, and on the third day arrived at the Red Sea. But God hardened Pharaoh's heart, and the Egyptians, forgetting the evils that had befallen them before, pursued the Israelites together with Pharaoh. Let no one suppose that Pharaoh was forced by God into blindness to what was happening; for whoever says such a thing is perhaps condemning God of injustice, saying: "If he himself hardens the heart, why does he find fault with the one who is hardened?" Let him know rather that the easing of the plagues became the cause of his hardening. Whenever God brought the blows upon him, he promised to release the people; but whenever God relieved him of the torments, he was hardened. This is exactly what Scripture means, word for word, when it says: "When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he made his heart heavy and did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said"; and: "For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show in you all my power." When you hear this, do not take it blasphemously, saying: "Why does he punish them, when he is preparing him to resist him? Why does he strike, if there is no injustice with God?" Let such a person know first that what seem to be contradictions in Scripture are resolved not by reasonings but by examples. Just as the best physicians, eager to discover something beneficial for human nature, ask for those who have been sentenced to death and dissect them, so that through those condemned to die they may find something beneficial to mankind, so God, who surpasses all human

wisdom, shows great signs through Pharaoh, who had sinned beyond cure: he punishes the one who deserved punishment, while healing those born afterward, making that man's punishment an occasion of salvation for them. So Pharaoh gathered all his forces, two hundred chariots and two hundred thousand horsemen, and pursued the Israelites. They, when the Red Sea had been divided by Moses at God's command, went on their way; and the Egyptians, driving after them, were drowned when Moses struck with the rod and brought the waters back together. On the following day the water, driven by the wind, carried the weapons of the Egyptians to the multitude of the Hebrews. Moses, judging that this too had come about by the providence of God, ordered them to take them up, so that they would not be unarmed. So they came into the desert. And Raguel, also called Jethro (for he had two names), came to Moses, bringing him his wife and sons; and when he learned from him all the wonders God had worked against the Egyptians, he was amazed and glorified God. He was, as they say, a descendant of Abraham, born of one of the sons Keturah bore him; for from Jokshan came Dedan, Raguel, Jethro and Hobab. So Moses received him with all kindness and sent him on his way to his own country. Moses himself, after giving many laws for the benefit of the Hebrews, died, having lived one hundred and twenty years; and Joshua son of Nun succeeded to his leadership and led the people out of the desert, where they had spent forty years and where traces of the Jews' habitation are still preserved. For those who have visited the places out of curiosity report that the outlines of the tents still remain, countless in number, and that one can see Mount Sinai, beside which Moses received the laws, and each of the things recorded in detail. But we must ask how the Hebrews sojourned in Egypt four hundred and thirty years and not two hundred and fifteen; for the consecutive record of the dates indicates two hundred and fifteen, but Scripture four hundred and thirty. For it says that the seed of Abraham will sojourn in a foreign land four hundred and thirty years. First, then, we should observe that it did not say "in Egypt," but that the seed of Abraham would sojourn in a foreign land. And the land of Canaan was also foreign, where Isaac sojourned, who above all others was the chosen seed of Abraham, for he was his son. It is clear, then, that before they inherited the land of the foreigners they were sojourners for up to four hundred and thirty years, as the Apostle also says somewhere: "A covenant previously ratified by God ... after four hundred and thirty years, so as to [?] the promise"; and he adds: "But God granted it to Abraham through a promise." It is likely, then, that they sojourned two hundred and fifteen years in Canaan, and in

Egypt the same two hundred and fifteen, which together make four hundred and thirty years. As Joshua was leading the people and the ark of the covenant across the Jordan, the waters stood apart in a single solid mass, standing very far off, while the water flowing down into the Salt Sea of the Arabah ran down until it failed entirely; and they all crossed on dry ground and encamped against Jericho. This city was fortified with very great walls. So they circled it for six days, as God had commanded; and on the seventh, at dawn, they went around it a seventh time, and the priests, blowing the trumpets, roused all the people to shout together; and as they [?], the wall at once fell, and the city was taken, and all of it was made an offering devoted to the Lord. After Jericho they laid an ambush for the city of Ai, and when they had taken it they burned it, and its king

[?] we were clothed, and we put new sandals on our feet; and the length of the road has worn all these out and made them old. So make peace with us and make us your friends." And the blessed Joshua confirmed peace with them by oaths. Later, when he discovered their cunning, he spared them because of the oath, but in return for their deceit [made them] carry wood and draw water for the Israelites

Adonibezek, king of Jerusalem, angry that the Gibeonites had deserted to the Israelites, took as allies the neighboring kings, Ailam king of Hebron, Phidon king of Jarmuth, Sipha king of Lachish, and also Dabir king of Odollam, encamped against them, and besieged Gibeon. The Gibeonites, hard pressed, sent envoys to Joshua. He was at Gilgal, and he drew up his army against them; and when battle was joined the foreigners were routed. Some were killed by the sword, others by hail; for as they fled, God rained down hail on them, which killed more of the enemy than the battle did. And so that he might destroy them completely, Joshua prayed to God to lengthen the day for them beyond the course of nature by stopping the sun over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Arnon. And God made the sun and the moon stand still, until the enemy had been overcome in the course of that one day.

Joshua son of Nun found the five kings of the nations hiding in a cave and ordered them to be thrown on their backs on the ground, and he had the people trample on their necks; [?] and after hanging their bodies on a tree, he later buried them in the cave. Having sacked all their cities, he subdued all the hill country and the plain. Then Asor, king of Iasin, taking the surrounding kings as allies, gathered a great force, so that the multitude of their army could be likened to the countless sand of the sea, and drew up against Joshua. But Joshua fell upon them suddenly and slaughtered him and all his allies with their entire army; he hamstrung their horses and distributed all their land among the Israelites. To the tribe of Reuben he allotted the land of the Amorites and Raphasen [?]; to Gad the same land of the Amorites, and he assigned it also to the half tribe of Manasseh; and to the tribe of Judah the land of the Hebrews [?], the Hittites, and the Anakim. The tribe of Judah, taking the tribe of Simeon as an ally, ravaged the Canaanites and Perizzites; and when they caught Adonibezek as he fled, they cut off the ends of his feet and hands. Lamenting his fate, he said: "As I have done, so God has repaid me. For seventy kings, with the ends of their feet and hands cut off, used to be under my table gathering up what fell from it." So he was brought to Jerusalem and died there at once. To the tribe of Ephraim Joshua assigned the land of the Amorites, the Perizzites and the Samaritans; and to the half tribe of Manasseh the land of the Gersaeans and the Amorites. The land of the Hebrews, the Amorites and the Jebusites he allotted to the tribe of Benjamin; to Simeon that of the Hebrews and the Perizzites; to Zebulun that of the Perizzites; that of the Kenites to Naphtali; to the tribe of Dan that of the Amorites; and to the tribe of Issachar and the tribe of Asher that of the Perizzites. Having distributed all this land, Joshua died at the age of one hundred and ten. When Eleazar son of Aaron died, his son Phinehas succeeded to the high priesthood. After the death of Joshua son of Nun, the Israelites fell away from God and served Astarte; and God delivered them into the hands of Chousarthan, king of the Syrians, who brought them into great distress, so that, after they had been long oppressed, they cried out to God, and there was given to them [?]
